title: Lecture #38: Lambdas & Functional Interface Deep Dive
topics: Core functional interfaces (Function, Consumer, Supplier, Predicate)

questions.question: In the lecture, `() -> Math.random()` was stored in a variable. Which `java.util.function` interface and abstract method fit the shape "takes nothing, returns a value" (void -> T)?
options: `Consumer<T>` with `void accept(T t)`
`Supplier<T>` with `T get()`
`Function<T, R>` with `R apply(T t)`
`Predicate<T>` with `boolean test(T t)`
questions.explanation: A Supplier takes no input and supplies a value through `get()`, which is exactly what `() -> Math.random()` does. Consumer is the opposite shape (T -> void): it takes a value and returns nothing.

questions.question: What does this predicate-combining program print?
options:
false
true

true
true

false
false

true
false
questions.explanation: For 56, `isGreater` is false, so the AND is false. For 57, both predicates are false, so the OR is false and `negate()` turns it into true. If you print "true" on the first line, you are treating `and()` like `or()`: 56 is even, but it is not greater than 100.

questions.question: A teammate wrote `list.forEach(x -> System.out.println(x));` and the code reviewer asks for a method reference instead. Which replacement compiles and does the same thing?
options: `list.forEach(System::println);`, a reference to `println` on the `System` class
`list.forEach(System.out.println);`, passing the method by its plain name
`list.forEach(System.out::println);`, a reference to `println` on the `System.out` object
`list.forEach(System.out::println(x));`, a reference that also passes the argument
questions.explanation: The syntax is `target::methodName`, with no parentheses or arguments. The target here is the `PrintStream` object `System.out`, so the reference is `System.out::println`, as in Demo2. `System::println` does not compile because `println` is not a method of the `System` class; it belongs to the `System.out` object.

questions.question: What does this composition demo print?
questions.explanation: `f.andThen(g)` means g(f(x)), so add2 runs first: (4 + 2) * 3 = 18. `f.compose(g)` means f(g(x)), so multiply3 runs first: 4 * 3 + 2 = 14. Answering 14 then 18 means the two methods were swapped.

questions.question: The notes point out that `Function<Integer, Integer> square = x -> x * x;` goes through "unboxing -> operation -> autoboxing" on every call. Why does `java.util.function` also provide interfaces like `IntUnaryOperator` and `IntPredicate`?
options: They work directly on primitive `int`/`long`/`double` values, so the boxing and unboxing overhead goes away
Generic interfaces like `Function` cannot be used with numbers at all, so primitive versions are mandatory for arithmetic
They are allowed to declare more than one abstract method, which makes them more flexible than `Function`
They make the lambda run on a separate thread, which speeds up numeric code
questions.explanation: Generics only work with reference types, so `Function<Integer, Integer>` has to box and unbox wrapper objects. The primitive specialisations take and return `int`, `long` or `double` directly and avoid that cost. They are not mandatory, though: `Function<Integer, Integer>` works fine with numbers through autoboxing, just less efficiently.

questions.question: You need a functional interface that takes a `String` and returns its length as a primitive `int`, without boxing the result. Using the naming scheme from the notes (`IntFunction` vs `ToIntFunction`), which one fits?
options: `IntFunction<String>`, because its method takes a `String` and returns an `int`
`Function<String, Integer>`, because it is the primitive version of `Function`
`ToIntFunction<String>`, because its `applyAsInt(String)` method returns a primitive `int`
`IntUnaryOperator`, because it is the `int -> int` operator
questions.explanation: `ToIntFunction<T>` maps T -> int, so `ToIntFunction<String> len = String::length;` returns a primitive. `IntFunction<R>` is the reverse shape (int -> R): its input is an `int`, so `IntFunction<String>` would turn an int into a String.

questions.question: The notes write `Predicate<String> p = String::isEmpty;` and then `p.test("Hello")` returns `false`. `isEmpty()` takes no arguments, so how is `test(String)` mapped onto it?
options: It is a static method reference, so `String.isEmpty("Hello")` is called
It refers to an instance method of an arbitrary object of type String: the argument to `test` becomes the receiver, so `"Hello".isEmpty()` is called
It is bound to one fixed String object chosen when the lambda is created, and `test`'s argument is ignored
It compiles only because `Predicate` has a special overload `test()` with no parameters
questions.explanation: `ClassName::instanceMethod` is an unbound reference: the first parameter of the functional method becomes the object the method is called on, so it is equivalent to `s -> s.isEmpty()`. It is not a static reference, because `isEmpty` is an instance method and no static `String.isEmpty(String)` exists.

questions.question: Which marked line fails to compile?
options: Line A
Line B
Line C
Line D
questions.explanation: `f.compose(g)` is f(g(x)): the input goes into g (String), and the result comes out of f (String), so its type is `Function<String, String>`. Line C is correct and Line D does not compile. Line A, g(f(x)), is Integer -> String -> Integer, so `Function<Integer, Integer>` is fine; picking it means mixing up the direction of andThen.

questions.question: A validation rule is built as `Predicate<String> valid = notEmpty.and(notNull);` where `notEmpty = s -> !s.isEmpty()` and `notNull = s -> s != null`. Calling `valid.test(null)` throws a `NullPointerException`. What is the correct fix?
options: Use `notEmpty.or(notNull)`, because `or()` never evaluates its first predicate when the input is null
Swap the order to `notNull.and(notEmpty)`, because `and()` short-circuits and skips the second predicate once the first returns false
Nothing can fix it with composition, because `and()` always evaluates both predicates, just like the `&` operator
Wrap it as `valid.negate().negate()`, because `negate()` filters out null inputs before testing
questions.explanation: The composed `and()` evaluates the left predicate first and skips the right one if the left is false. Putting `notNull` first means `isEmpty()` is never called on null. The idea that `and()` always evaluates both sides is a common misconception: the Javadoc says it is a short-circuiting logical AND, like `&&`.

questions.question: The notes show `Supplier<List<Integer>> s = ArrayList::new;`. Suppose instead you write `Function<Integer, List<String>> make = ArrayList::new;`. Which constructor does the reference use, and what does `make.apply(10).size()` return?
options: `ArrayList(int initialCapacity)` is used, so the list has capacity 10 but `size()` returns 0
`ArrayList()` is used and 10 is added as the first element, so `size()` returns 1
`ArrayList(Collection)` is used, so the call throws `ClassCastException` and `size()` is never reached
`ArrayList(int initialCapacity)` is used and filled with 10 null slots, so `size()` returns 10
questions.explanation: A constructor reference chooses the constructor that matches the functional method's parameters. `apply(Integer)` matches `ArrayList(int)` through unboxing, so 10 becomes the initial capacity. Capacity is not size: a new list holds no elements, so `size()` is 0, not 10.
